body:
For example, on [DuckDuckGo](http://duckduckgo.com/) they have instructions that include clicking a button that invokes `AddSearchProvider`.  But that step is actually completely unnecessary in Chrome because the mere presence of the `<link rel="search">` tag has already added the provider (and all that remains in their instructions is for the user to mark that provider as the default).

So is there really any value to having an imperative API that says when this should be done (which is subject to abuse), when we already have a declarative API that leaves the timing up to the user / UA?

I realized we never responded to this. Very sorry about that! I think if the Chrome removal goes through with no problems, it would make sense to remove this API. @smaug----, any objections from Gecko, who would be the only remaining supporter?

Testing Edge, it looks like in F12 developers tools, `window.external` exists as a getter that always returns a new empty object, so that `window.external !== window.external`. However, my jsbin always returns `undefined`, so... that's weird. @DigiTec @travisleithead, any comments?

http://jsbin.com/kizilemusi/edit?html,console,output shows output in mobile Chrome and mobile/desktop Firefox, but undefined in mobile Safari and in Edge. Mobile Chrome does not have `window.External` with a capital `E`, interestingly.

Is Blink planning to just completely remove `window.external`? That would be nice :).

As a platform, we still need window.external. It is currently the way that a host extends the namespace and provides host specific augmentations. We support this through a foreignObject type (IDispatch) instead of a native type. We've been thinking and I have the code for, turning this into a native type which forwards to the underlying control instead. This is why it looks weird for you.

Do we support AddSearchProvider? We do, but its no-op. In other words, you can call it and it won't throw. 

Do we support a prototype for the External object? No. 

Do we support getting back a function as a property (aka as a Function)? No.

So we've already deprecated AddSearchProvider by simply having it be no-op, but we know websites that DO break if we remove it entirely. This is what caused us to add it back in.

So what explains the web-exposed behavior of `window.external` being `undefined`? Is it another `document.all`?

I don't think the platform needs an extension point for nonstandard behaviors in this manner, so I'm not too concerned about that. If Edge does that, then it's outside standards and not part of the web platform.

But if there's a compatibility risks of sites breaking if we just remove `window.external` and its methods that's worth knowing, and we'll have to make them no-ops per spec.

> So what explains the web-exposed behavior of window.external being undefined? Is it another document.all?

For Edge it should be returning an object. At least in my local builds window.external is returning an empty object as is `typeof window.external` returning "object".

I know for some period of time we had a weird behavior in Chakra where typeof on HostDispatch would return "undefined" in SOME modes but right now I can't even confirm that in my Windows 10 IE 11. I'm always getting object back now.

That said, yes, we did have multiple sites that would not work because they blindly called AddSearchProvider without any checks. So removing it would cause an unsupported property or method exception to get thrown.

I'm not proposing that we have strange behavior, in fact I think we'll eventually add the interface External per the spec. Ours will simply be a PlatformObject which means it can have its own properties and methods meaning we need to build the namespace resolver that allows the host to extend it. I don't think any of that is non-standard really.

> For Edge it should be returning an object.

Hmm OK. It looks like `window.external` is weird in various ways that break loggers in jsbin and live-dom-viewer so I'll chalk it up to that.

> Ours will simply be a PlatformObject which means it can have its own properties and methods meaning we need to build the namespace resolver that allows the host to extend it. I don't think any of that is non-standard really.

Well, if it has properties and methods that are not in the spec, that's nonstandard.

Fine ;-) yes, the specific properties and methods would not be per spec. Not much different than adding stuff to navigator and then floating the standards later though ;-) Or the chrome namespace! Its useful to have a place where the "Browser" is allowed to put stuff that might relate to platform specific or host specific behaviors. Though I totally agree that the extensions are not a standard and its a risky, slippery slope.

Well, why add External interface if we actually would like to get rid of it.
Adding any properties to window.external which aren't specified by some web spec is non-standard, not
any better than some random vendor-prefixed properties. 
(But just like random properties in window.external are non-standard, so is the whole window.chrome and hopefully certain browsers get rid of that.)

> Its useful to have a place where the "Browser" is allowed to put stuff that might relate to platform specific or host specific behaviors.

Why is it useful? That is not how the platform should work that vendors can dump random APIs there.

> Why is it useful? 

Our example would be we use it for resource pages and providing protected APIs (as a form of host extensible configurable type system) so that the browser can ship improvements outside of the platform revving. We think we can come up with better long term solutions, but for now this is really efficient and derives from the web of 1995, so its been around FOREVER.

But anyhow about this bug. It is rather difficult to have any useful numbers about the use of the API. Users add new search providers very rarely, so of course AddSearchProvider would get super low usage. I'm a bit worried about some odd intranet usage and what not. But if everyone else manages to remove it, Gecko will follow I think. At least we could add some note to MDN and the HTML spec that the feature is deprecated.

Does this bug apply to  IsSearchProviderInstalled too?

It looks like @evanstade is the initiator of [the blink-dev thread](https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/forum/#!msg/blink-dev/FXZloLz3Bao/a12qrjubCAAJ). He says he'll be adding use counters for both. It sounds like based on Edge's research though that the use counters are not likely to come out in favor of removing it, and instead they might need to get specced as no-ops :(

I'm not sure if these use counters have reached stable yet but chromestatus shows [<0.0001% usage for AddSearchProvider](https://www.chromestatus.com/metrics/feature/timeline/popularity/981) but [0.0019% usage for IsSearchProviderInstalled](https://www.chromestatus.com/metrics/feature/timeline/popularity/982).
Per current spec AddSearchProvider can be no-op

Adding more data. We actually have a gallery that allows people to install search providers. Of course, in Edge this doesn't work, but still does for IE.

https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/iegallery

Also, AddSearchProvider is a customer ask from time to time, including some press and influentials. I'm still working on getting a site list. We also, unfortunately, can't use counter a foreignObject, but that would be super cool. If we made it native we could. I'll put that information in the bug/work item and see if it changes minds.

@DigiTec do you have examples where customers really wanted `AddSearchProvider` for scenarios where `<link rel=search>` wasn't sufficient?  We couldn't find any compelling ones (and our even asking this question [led at least one search engine](https://groups.google.com/a/chromium.org/d/msg/blink-dev/FXZloLz3Bao/R8m_NEs6DwAJ) to switch to `link` to get better UX).

I agree it's very unlikely we'd want to remove these APIs, just stub them out to always return (as alowed by the spec) their default values.  But maybe the spec should be updated anyway to somehow indicated that the APIs are officially deprecated, possibly even defined to ONLY return constants?

We did our digging so hopefully this gives you guys enough data:
1. We do no-op it and have since Edge has shipped.
2. We did try to remove it, but broke, from what I can tell now, only MS properties, which we can get fixed. At the time, the data was causal enough for us to take a fix. Now, that said, we still want to be prudent here and rely on use counters to validate our assumptions. We could certainly rely on Chrome's counters here.
3. If the decision was made to remove these APIs we could do that, but we still have more APIs on external (as provided by the host) that we can't remove. Some of which are for critical things where browsers' disagree (such as networking provisioning for which we all have our own standards I'm told). So a higher level decision to go and remove the External interface and the external property altogether would be a second decision process.

For the compat story. Edge does not support nor IE, the normal ability to feature detect APIs on this object so you have to call them. Which means if you want to use them you have to wrap them in try/catch in case they don't exist. I'm not sure how many sites would have been properly written to deal with the rather odd behaviors of the external object, nor how many even try to feature detect these APIs rather than blindly call them.

The exception to this is the `in` operator. You can do `"AddSearchProvider" in window.external` and that should work. Ex:

``` javascript
"AddSearchProvider" in window.external
// returns true
window.external.AddSearchProvider
// throws Invalid procedure call or argument
```

@RByers Yes the use case was to build stores like https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/iegallery for search providers for which there are maybe better ways now. We also had an IE test drive demo that used the feature (so that was the two sites). Because they were both MS sites and fairly heavily trafficked it generated a lot of feedback from customers that relied on them for their search provider workflow.

@DigiTec does Edge have the same behavior as Chrome where `<link rel=search>` entries are automatically added exactly like `AddSearchProvider` does?  I can see arguments against that design, but it seems to have worked out well for us so far. 

If browsers agree on it, then I think the stores scenario is strictly a better experience when leveraging `<link>`: it's the web so there's no need to "add" anything, your "store" is just a list of links, and after you visit one you have the search provider available just as if you had "added" it.
@RByers I actually don't know the answer to that! I'll ask around and report back.

@RByers We have a less inclusive policy, but we do collect <link rel="search"> and that is how we enable open search providers in Microsoft Edge. I also got confirmation from the main Browser team that owns this experience and they have no interest in supporting/adding back in this API. They can achieve the experiences they want without it.

@DigiTec, cool thanks!

So does everyone agree then that we should just stub out these APIs in the spec to just return constants?

We return `undefined` for `AddSearchProvider` and `2` for `IsSearchProviderInstalled` as reference. Not sure if that is what everyone returns though. We do no parameter validation so there are no parameter combos that would cause the results to different. Our comment for why 2, though its probably just wishful thinking. We did have a very long email thread about what this value should be and we decided 2 to dissuade websites who used the API from trying to constantly tell you to add their search provider.

``` c
// return 2 (The specified search provider is installed and is set as the default search provider) to achieve better compatibility on old webpages
```
